rows.speaker: Aj, IK, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Aj, IK, R, and Ṭ explain that no one bears another person’s sins or duties.
rows.anchor: no one will bear the sins or duties of others (Aj, IK, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Aj reads the rule that each bears their own burden as a manifestation of God’s Justice.
rows.anchor: points to God’s Justice (Aj).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q understands the phrase as opening a new discussion.
rows.anchor: the introduction of a new discussion (Q)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R connects it to the prior description of human poverty before God: people cannot assume or transfer burdens because they lack power to decide such matters.
rows.anchor: one cannot take on the burden of another or cast one’s burden upon another (R)

rows.speaker: Commentators
rows.claim: Commentators reconcile 29:13 by taking leaders’ own burdens as the consequences of their own being misled, and others’ burdens as the consequences of misleading them.
rows.anchor: Commentators reconcile this phrase with 29:13, Surely they will bear their own burdens

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK explains that whoever does good deeds receives their benefit.
rows.anchor: whoever performs good deeds receives the benefit of those deeds (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse presents moral reflexivity: good and evil actions ultimately affect the person who performs them.
rows.anchor: This verse thus demonstrates a moral reflexivity in which the ultimate impact of actions, good or bad, is always upon the one who performs

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ identifies the living as people whose hearts are alive with faith and the dead as people whose hearts are dead under disbelief; this answers questions in 6:122 and 39:22.
rows.anchor: those who hear the truth of the revelation, while those whose hearts are buried in the grave of ignorance cannot hear it (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Aj explains God’s causing people to hear as His guiding and supporting them.
rows.anchor: God’s causing them to hear thus refers to His guiding them and supporting them (Aj)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK reads the different colors as the diversity of human races and ethnicities, linked to 30:22.
rows.anchor: the variation in your tongues and colors (IK)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q also reads the differences as variations in people’s inner states.
rows.anchor: inner states of human beings differ (Q)

words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: IK, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: IK, Q, and Ṭ take those who know to mean those who know that God has power over all things.
rows.anchor: God is Powerful over all things (IK, Q, Ṭ)

words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that the person with the greatest knowledge of God fears Him most intensely.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said, “The one among you

words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R takes the verse to show that knowledge is superior to worship.
rows.anchor: the superiority of knowledge over worship (R)

words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A famous hadith says the knowledge seeker is guided toward the Garden, angels and creatures seek forgiveness for the learned, and the learned inherit prophetic knowledge and outrank worshippers.
rows.anchor: as in a famous ḥadīth: “Whosoever sets upon a path to seek knowledge, God will set him upon a path to the Garden.

words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Bḍ notes that the following mention of obligatory worship shows knowledge must be joined to worship and embodied in action to benefit its possessor.
rows.anchor: demonstrates that such knowledge must be combined with worship and manifest in one’s actions in order to be of benefit (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that the condemned do not die resembles 20:74, which says the guilty neither die nor live in Hell.
rows.anchor: They will neither be done away with so as to die is similar to 20:74

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment is not eased after sentence because disbelievers already received worldly respite and repeated opportunities to repent; related passages likewise deny relief or respite.
rows.anchor: they had already been granted respite and thus had many opportunities to repent during the life of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises that whenever the punishment abates, the disbelievers will receive an increase of blazing flame.
rows.anchor: Every time it abates, We shall increase for them a blazing flame (17:97; cf. 78:30)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse follows the counsel to warn and leave disbelievers to their choices: their wrongdoing will be reckoned at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: the price of their wrongdoing will come due upon the Resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving life to the dead can refer to the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: can be seen as a reference to the Resurrection

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK reads giving life to the dead as God reviving the earth after its death.
rows.anchor: to God’s bringing the earth back to life, as in 57:17: Know that God revives the earth after its death (IK)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z reads it as God bringing people from idolatry to faith.
rows.anchor: bringing people from idolatry to faith (Z)

rows.speaker: Aj, IK
rows.claim: Aj and IK read it as reviving hearts deadened by heedlessness and ignorance through knowledge and truth.
rows.anchor: the revivification, through knowledge and truth, of hearts made dead through heedlessness and ignorance (Aj, IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What people sent forth means deeds that will testify for or against them in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: refers to the deeds that will testify for or against them in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What people leave behind literally means their footsteps or traces.
rows.anchor: literally means “their footsteps” or “their traces.”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Banū Salimah, settled far from the mosque, wanted to move nearer; after the verse was revealed, the Prophet said their rewarded footprints were recorded and asked why they wished to move.
rows.anchor: So the Prophet said to them, “Your footprints are recorded

rows.speaker: Aj, Ṭ
rows.claim: Aj and Ṭ understand the traces more broadly as good deeds one leaves behind.
rows.anchor: the traces of good deeds that one leaves behind (Aj, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A well-known hadith says the dead person’s deeds end except beneficial knowledge, a righteous child’s prayer, and ongoing charity left behind.
rows.anchor: As a well-known ḥadīth states, “When the son of Adam dies, all his deeds come to an end except three:

rows.speaker: Aj, Ṭb, Ṭs
rows.claim: Aj, Ṭb, and Ṭs read the clear registry as the Preserved Tablet, the leader of other books, containing God’s decrees.
rows.anchor: all things from the beginning of time to its end on the Preserved Tablet (85:22; Aj, Ṭb, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Aj, IK, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Aj, IK, Q, and Ṭs instead take the clear imam as the book or registry recording human actions.
rows.anchor: Others say imām refers to the book or “registry” in which all human actions are recorded (Aj, IK, Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Shiite theologians
rows.claim: Shiite theologians cite the verse as Quranic support for divinely ordained imamate after the Prophet’s death.
rows.anchor: cited by Shiite theologians as Quranic support for the Shiite understanding of Divinely ordained leadership

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: Al-Qummī reports ʿAlī saying he is the clear imam who distinguishes truth from falsehood and inherited the office from the Messenger.
rows.anchor: al-Qummī relates a saying from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib: “I, by God, am the clear imām

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Shiite sources report the Prophet saying that ʿAlī is the Imam in whom God records knowledge of all things.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said regarding ʿAlī,“He is the Imam in whom God records the knowledge of all things” (Qm, Ṭb)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q explains the lunar mansions as the Moon’s waxing and waning through twenty-eight stations during one lunar month.
rows.anchor: of a single lunar month (Q)

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: Q and Z explain the old palm stalk as the withered remains of a date cluster, resembling a thin crescent in shape, width, and color.
rows.anchor: the thin crescent moon in shape, width, and color (Q, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse returns to the sūrah’s opening discussion of revelation and recalls the accusations that Muhammad was a poet.
rows.anchor: the nature of revelation from the beginning of the sūrah

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: IK and Q report that the Prophet had no facility with poetry, including its rhyme or meter.
rows.anchor: the Prophet did not have any facility with poetry, either its rhyme or meter (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charge that Muhammad authored the Quran is answered at 29:48: he had not recited a book or written with his right hand.
rows.anchor: Regarding the accusations that the Prophet had himself authored the Quran, 29:48 replies

words: إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌۭ وَقُرْءَانٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is repeatedly described as a reminder in 6:69, 6:90, 12:104, 38:87, 68:52, 74:31, and 81:27.
rows.anchor: That the Quran is but a reminder is repeated in several verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reminding is revelation’s function: the Torah is a Reminder, and Jews and Christians are called the people of the Reminder.
rows.anchor: To remind is the function of all revelation; hence the Torah is called a Reminder (40:54)

words: إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌۭ وَقُرْءَانٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran continues earlier Reminders and clarifies what people may have forgotten; 16:44 says it was sent down to clarify revelation for mankind.
rows.anchor: the Quran is presented as a continuation of the previous Reminders that clarifies what humans may have forgotten from them

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK takes warning those who are alive to mean all humanity, as in the Quran’s warning to its hearers and whomever it reaches.
rows.anchor: all of humanity, as in 6:19: And this Quran has been revealed unto me, that thereby I may warn you and whomsoever it may reach (IK)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q takes those who are alive as people whose hearts live and can hear the warning and soften at God’s remembrance.
rows.anchor: those whose hearts are alive (Q) and thus able to hear the warning and soften unto the remembrance of God (39:23)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the meaning of the Word coming due for disbelievers, the commentary refers to 36:7.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of the Word coming due, see 36:7c.

rows.speaker: IJ, IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The believer asks his companions in the Garden to look.
rows.anchor: The believer then says to his companions in the Garden, Will you look? (IJ, IK, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer sees his worldly companion in Hell and realizes he would have shared his fate had he followed him; God’s guidance saved him.
rows.anchor: had he followed him, he would have suffered the same fate and that if not for God’s Blessing in guiding him

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr glosses the passage with 7:43, where believers credit God with guiding them and say they would not have been guided otherwise.
rows.anchor: Thus Ibn Kathīr glosses these verses with 7:43, where the believers say

rows.speaker: the Biblical book of Jonah
rows.claim: The Biblical account says Jonah fled God’s presence, a tempest struck the ship, sailors cast lots and identified him, and eventually threw him overboard, calming the sea.
rows.anchor: According to the Biblical book of Jonah, Jonah, having fled “from the presence of the Lord”

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK reports that some Quranic commentators say the hesitant sailors watched Jonah throw himself into the fish’s mouth when it rose by God’s command.
rows.anchor: the fish’s mouth when it rose, by God’s Command, to carry him away (IK)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Different accounts keep Jonah in the fish for three, seven, or forty days; another says he was swallowed in the morning and expelled that evening.
rows.anchor: he was swallowed in the morning and cast out in the evening (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah was blameworthy because he fled Nineveh.
rows.anchor: Jonah was blameworthy for having fled Nineveh.

rows.speaker: Kisāʾī, Qiṣaṣ al-anbiyāʾ
rows.claim: Kisāʾī says the Ninevites beat Jonah as he called them to repent; after preaching for forty days, they dismissed him as mad.
rows.anchor: he continued preaching to them for forty days, but they dismissed him as mad (Kisāʾī, Qiṣaṣal-anbiyāʾ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After God sent Jonah to watch the expected punishment, the Ninevites repented and were spared; Jonah left angry, thinking God had no power over him.
rows.anchor: Jonah went away in anger, and thought We had no power over him (21:87)

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some say Jonah fled because he was angry that the Ninevites escaped punishment for rejecting him.
rows.anchor: Some say that he was angry that they were not punished for having rejected him

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: IK and Ṭ say Jonah’s prior life of devotion prevented him from remaining in the fish until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: Had it not been for the life of devotion lived before these events, Jonah would have remained in the belly of the fish (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: the Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying urges people to know God in ease, so God will aid them in difficulty.
rows.anchor: a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, “Seek to know God in times of ease, and He will know you

rows.speaker: Aj, IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Aj, IK, and Ṭ also understand the glorifiers as referring to Jonah’s prayer in the darkness, declaring God’s oneness and glorifying Him (21:87).
rows.anchor: (21:87; Aj, IK, Ṭ); for the more extensive prayer and repentance of Jonah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary notes that Jonah’s prayer and repentance are more extensively related in the Biblical book of Jonah 2:1–9.
rows.anchor: for the more extensive prayer and repentance of Jonah in the Bible, see Jonah 2:1–9

words: لَلَبِثَ فِى بَطْنِهِۦٓ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ
rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Aj says that without his praise, Jonah would have remained alive in the fish until human beings were resurrected.
rows.anchor: the belly of the fish alive until the day on which human beings are resurrected (Aj)

words: لَلَبِثَ فِى بَطْنِهِۦٓ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ
rows.speaker: Aj, Ṭ
rows.claim: Aj and Ṭ offer another reading: the fish’s belly would have served as Jonah’s grave until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: the belly of the fish would have been his grave until the Day of Resurrection (Aj, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṭāghūt denotes false authorities, objects of worship, and causes; shunning such sources concerns rejecting worship of whatever is other than God.
rows.anchor: False deities translates al-ṭāghūt, which denotes a variety of false sources of authority, false objects of worship, and false causes

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ says shunning false deities entails avoiding worship of everything other than God.
rows.anchor: shunning the worship of all that is other than God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ reports that some take al-ṭāghūt as singular and identify it with Satan.
rows.anchor: Some take al-ṭāghūt to be singular and thus understand it to mean Satan (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK explains that they understand the Word and act in accordance with it, like Moses’ instruction to hold firmly to the best of the Torah’s commandments.
rows.anchor: Those who listen to the Word, then follow are those who understand it and act in accord with it (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They possess intellect because they follow and act in accordance with revelation.
rows.anchor: They are possessors of intellect because they follow and act in accord with revelation

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z reads following the most beautiful as distinguishing good from best and virtuous from most virtuous, then choosing what is closer to God and earns greater reward.
rows.anchor: chooses the best or most virtuous course of action, desiring what is closer to God and what merits greater reward (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of God sending water from the sky is connected to 6:99.
rows.anchor: God’s sending down water from the sky

words: ثُمَّ يُخْرِجُ بِهِۦ زَرْعًۭا مُّخْتَلِفًا أَلْوَٰنُهُۥ ثُمَّ يَهِيجُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stages of plant life serve as a metaphor for the stages of human life, as in 18:45 and 57:20.
rows.anchor: the various stages of plant life are posed as a metaphor for the stages of human life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired parables show God’s power over all things and that all things perish except God’s Face.
rows.anchor: Both verses indicate God’s Power over all things and that all things perish, save His Face (28:88)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God takes souls by sending the Angel of Death, as stated in 32:11.
rows.anchor: God takes souls by sending the Angel of Death to them, as in 32:11

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R says souls are completely separated from the body in death and partially separated in sleep.
rows.anchor: In death souls are completely detached from the body, and in sleep they are partially detached (R)

rows.speaker: aḥādīth
rows.claim: Aḥādīth call sleep the brother of death and say the people of the Garden do not die.
rows.anchor: Sleep is the brother of death, and the people of the Garden do not die” (Q)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet taught a bedtime prayer asking God to show mercy if He takes the sleeper’s soul and to protect it if He returns it.
rows.anchor: the Prophet advised his Companions to say when going to bed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed term can mean death or the Day of Judgment, when all things return to God.
rows.anchor: A term appointed indicates the moment of death or the Day of Judgment, when all things are returned to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every human being and all creation have a decreed term.
rows.anchor: For all human beings, as for all creation, this term is decreed, as in 6:2

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R takes the appointed term here as the waking return of souls to bodies, granting reprieve until death and reckoning.
rows.anchor: till a term appointed refers to the return of souls to their bodies when they awaken (R)
